about: The narration's cast: one voice per speaker key in data/narration (an ArchitectKey, or guide). Each voice is made by a voice-design TTS from its brief, matched to the architect's portrait; target is the pitch (Hz, median) and pace (words a minute) the brief asks for, checked by scripts/narration/measure.py. line is what auditions speak: the speaker's own script text, or for an architect with no script yet, their note in lib/architects.ts in the first person. Pitch and pace are said outright in every brief: left to words like 'alto', the model ran higher and quicker than asked.

guide.name: The guide
guide.brief: A contemporary Californian woman of about 40 with a low, warm alto voice, lower-pitched than most women. She speaks slowly and steadily, unhurried, calm and close to the ear, like a good museum guide: plain facts, gently told, with a little warmth and no performance. Never bright, high or salesy.
guide.line: This is the commercial heart of the city: the civic buildings around the park, the banks and the grand hotel on Shattuck Avenue, and the Art Deco library.

maybeck.name: Bernard Maybeck
maybeck.brief: An American man of about 80 with a soft, airy baritone and a faint old-world lilt. He speaks slowly and warmly, smiling as he talks, a chuckle never far away, with small pauses of wonder between ideas. Gentle and romantic, delighted by ordinary materials. Close and intimate, never booming.
maybeck.line: The Christian Scientists asked me for a church in 1910. Most of their churches were plain and classical, as rational as the faith. I wanted this one to feel like what happens inside it.

morgan.name: Julia Morgan
morgan.brief: A Californian woman of about 50 with a light, clear mezzo voice, mid-pitched. Quiet and exact: precise consonants, an even, measured pace, no wasted words. Reserved and businesslike, with a dry wit she never underlines. Warm underneath but never effusive; she lets the building speak.
morgan.line: This was St. John's Presbyterian Church. Its congregation formed in 1907, some of them families who had lost their homes in San Francisco the year before, and they wanted a church for the lowest possible price.

howard.name: John Galen Howard
howard.brief: An American man of about 55 with a deep, resonant bass-baritone and formal East-coast diction, rounded vowels. He speaks slowly and deliberately, building each sentence to land, like a professor addressing a full hall. Grand but not pompous, warming when he speaks of his own house. Early twentieth-century polish.
howard.line: This was my own house. I built it in 1912 on the corner of Le Roy Avenue and Rose Street, and we called it Rose Le Roy. By then I had been the university's supervising architect for eleven years.

ratcliff.name: Walter H. Ratcliff Jr.
ratcliff.brief: An American man of about 40 with a bright, clean light-tenor voice and a smile you can hear. Brisk and friendly, a quick walking pace, as if alongside you; plain-spoken and practical, proud of his town without boasting. Neighbourly, cheerful, easy to follow.
ratcliff.line: I was Berkeley's first city architect, and I spent most of my working life in this town. In 1925 the Central Berkeley Building Company asked me for something Berkeley had never had: a tall building.

hays.name: William Charles Hays
hays.brief: An American man of about 60 with a lean, dry baritone, slightly nasal and very precise. He speaks deliberately, at an unhurried pace, with crisp consonants: the patient exactness of a professor who has explained this for forty years. A wry undertone, never a joke spelled out.
hays.line: I taught architecture at the university for nearly forty years, and I designed buildings for it too.

coxhead.name: Ernest Coxhead
coxhead.brief: An Englishman of about 65 with a low, quiet baritone and an older southern English accent. He speaks slowly and with restraint, with a church architect's reverence and a little gruffness at the edges. Clipped where it counts; dry humour held well back.
coxhead.line: I trained in England as an architect of churches. In 1886 my brother Almeric and I set up practice in Los Angeles, and four years later we moved to San Francisco.

thomas.name: John Hudson Thomas
thomas.brief: An American man of about 40 with a bright, lively baritone and a grin in his voice. He talks quickly, ideas tumbling out, inventive and pleased with the rule he is about to break. Playful and a little mischievous, but always clear.
thomas.line: I designed houses, mostly, and I liked to mix things that weren't supposed to go together: Arts and Crafts with the Vienna Secession, the medieval with the new.

plachek.name: James W. Plachek
plachek.brief: An American man of about 45 with a smooth, warm, fairly low baritone and polished 1930s diction, clean as a radio announcer. Confident and civic-minded, at an easy, even pace, quietly proud, glad to show you around downtown. Assured without swagger.
plachek.line: If you've walked around downtown, you've walked past my work: the annex behind the old City Hall, the Odd Fellows' Temple on Fulton Street, the Corder Building down at Bancroft. But this is the one I'd want you to see.

gutterson.name: Henry Gutterson
gutterson.brief: An American man of about 60 with a mellow, low baritone and a soft gravel, a pipe smoker's warmth. Easygoing and content, he speaks slowly, in no hurry at all, generous with credit to others. Relaxed, close, companionable.
gutterson.line: I trained in the Beaux-Arts way, and I worked alongside Bernard Maybeck. The Berkeley Community Theater is mine.

yelland.name: William R. Yelland
yelland.brief: A Californian man of about 35 with a light, bright tenor that ranges widely in pitch. Theatrical and full of wonder, a storyteller who paints pictures as he goes, at a lively pace, delighted by fairy-tale roofs; charming, never arch.
yelland.line: I grew up in Saratoga, studied architecture at the University here, and then the war sent me to France. I came home with Normandy in my head, the farmhouses and steep roofs and old brick, and I never quite got it out.

esherick.name: Joseph Esherick
esherick.brief: A West Coast American man of about 65 with a dry, understated mid baritone and a little gravel. Laconic and conversational, at a relaxed pace, the modernist professor who says less than he knows. Cool and plainspoken, late twentieth century; no flourish.
esherick.line: I was a modernist of the Bay tradition, and I taught at Berkeley for a long time. Greenwood Common is mine, and the Sea Ranch.
